title: The Rule of 72: Why a Few Percentage Points Change Everything
description:
There's a shortcut for figuring out how long it takes money to double, no calculator needed. We use it to show why the gap between a 2% savings account and a 10% index fund isn't small - it's the difference between doubling once and doubling five times.

This video uses AI-generated narration and visuals.

#ruleof72 #investing #personalfinance

segments.text: Want to know how many years it takes your money to double? There's a shortcut simple enough to do in your head.
It's called the Rule of 72. Divide 72 by your annual interest rate, and you get roughly how many years until your money doubles.
The gap between a decent rate and a mediocre one isn't small. It's the difference between doubling five times or barely doubling once.
At two percent, doubling takes thirty-six years. At six percent, twelve years. At ten percent, about seven.
Here's what that actually looks like with real money. Ten thousand dollars, growing at six percent, left completely alone.
Every twelve years or so, it roughly doubles again. By year forty-eight, that's four doublings - and a very different number.
The rate doesn't just add up over time. It multiplies. That's why a couple of extra percentage points matters more than people think.
The Rule of 72 isn't a trick. It's just what compounding looks like, sped up.
